problem: Deep-RL navigation agents had only been shown in small, visually simple simulators such as mazes, games and indoor houses. Most navigation systems depend on explicit maps, GPS or external memory. It was unclear whether end-to-end RL from raw images could handle city-scale, real-world visual navigation to goals kilometres away, or transfer across cities.
motivation: Humans learn to navigate cities from visual landmarks without maps or GPS. Photorealistic but small indoor environments and synthetic simulators lack the diversity of the real world (weather, pedestrians, vehicles, large extent). The authors observe that city navigation needs both general skills (vision, movement primitives) and locale-specific memorised knowledge (landmarks, topology), which suggests keeping these in separate network pathways.
key_idea: Build StreetLearn, an interactive RL environment on Google Street View panoramas, and solve its goal-driven 'courier' task with a dual-pathway recurrent agent: a city-specific goal LSTM interprets a landmark-based goal code and memorises the locale, and a shared policy LSTM plus convnet learn general navigation that transfers when only a new goal LSTM is trained.
insight: Separating locale-specific memory (goal LSTM) from general policy (convnet + policy LSTM) lets the agent memorise large city graphs and enables modular transfer. Freezing the convnet and policy LSTM after pre-training on 4 Manhattan regions and training only a new goal LSTM on Wall Street reaches performance comparable to joint training on all regions, and transfer improves with the number of pre-training regions (Fig. 6b). Ablations (Fig. 7) show three things: the auxiliary heading-prediction task clearly helps learning; the skip connection from the convnet to the policy LSTM helps single-city training but hurts multi-city transfer, since the bottleneck regularises the interface; and the goal-less and no-vision agents perform poorly, so success is not just street-graph exploration. Reward-shaping experiments (Fig. 3c) show two further points: random 'coins' do not help, and large early-reward radii make the task easy. A curriculum on goal distance plus small 200 m shaping is preferred because it keeps training consistent with test and avoids degenerate gradient-following. Held-out-goal tests (Table 1) show the landmark goal code interpolates only locally: test reward drops as the held-out areas grow, while half-trip time stays similar.
method: StreetLearn environment: a Google Street View panorama graph (e.g. NYU 17,227 nodes, Central London 24,428, Paris Rive Gauche 34,026, 5 Manhattan regions, ~10 m node spacing, up to 5 km extent). The agent sees an 84x84 RGB crop of a 60° view.
Action space: 5 discrete actions, rotate ±22.5° or ±67.5°, or move forward along the most central graph edge in the view cone (a no-op if no edge is in view).

Landmark goal code: goal g_t is a softmax over negative scaled distances (α=0.002) from the goal lat/long to 644 fixed manually defined landmarks. It is coordinate-free and scalable, and matches lat/long scalar inputs in ablations.

Courier task: random start pose; a goal is reached within 100 m, then a new goal is sampled. Episodes last 1000 steps. The goal reward is proportional to the shortest-path distance at assignment. Early reward shaping applies within 200 m and is given once per node, only while distance decreases.

CityNav architecture: a 2-layer convnet (8x8/4 with 16 maps, 4x4/2 with 32 maps) and FC-256 feed a goal LSTM (256 units, also receives g_t) whose tanh/dropout/64-d bottleneck output goes to a policy LSTM (256 units, also receives skip visual features, previous action and reward). The policy LSTM outputs the policy and value. Heading is predicted as an auxiliary 16-bin classification from the goal LSTM. The baseline GoalNav instead feeds g_t directly to a single LSTM.
MultiCityNav and transfer: one goal-LSTM pathway per city or region with a shared convnet and policy LSTM. For a new city, the convnet and policy LSTM are frozen and only a new goal LSTM is trained.

Training: IMPALA actor-critic with 256 actors for CityNav and 512 for MultiCityNav, unroll 50, RMSProp at lr 0.001 annealed over 2B (NYU), 4B (London) or 8B (multi-city) steps. The curriculum samples goals within 500 m, then grows the radius to the full graph (3.5–5 km).

setting.backbone: small conv encoder + goal LSTM + policy LSTM (CityNav/MultiCityNav), trained from scratch with RL (IMPALA)
setting.training_data: Online RL in StreetLearn (Google Street View panorama graphs of NYC Manhattan regions, Central London, Paris Rive Gauche). Billions of environment steps (e.g. 2B NYU, 4B London, 8B multi-city/transfer). No human demonstrations; compass heading used as an auxiliary training label.
setting.observation: monocular RGB (84x84 crop of a 60° view from a Street View panorama) + landmark-based absolute goal code (644-d) + previous action and reward
setting.action_space: 5 discrete actions on the panorama graph: rotate ±22.5°, rotate ±67.5°, move forward to the next connected panorama
setting.privileged: No map, GPS or pose for the agent at test time. The goal is given as an absolute code built from distances between the true goal lat/long and 644 fixed landmarks. Heading labels are used only as a training auxiliary.

numbers_note: The main courier-task results (NYU, London, Paris), the architecture ablations, reward-shaping and goal-representation studies, and the multi-city transfer results appear only as learning curves (Figs. 3, 6b, 7, 8), with no numeric tables. Table 1 (held-out goals) is the only table. Its metrics are average per-episode goal rewards, % missed goals (Fail) and half-trip time in steps (T1/2). The city region used for Table 1 is not explicitly stated. There are no SR/SPL metrics, and nothing comparable to StreetNav, Touchdown or other benchmarks.
results: CityNav, trained with a curriculum and 200 m early rewards, learns the courier task over multi-km goals in NYU, London and Paris. It reaches higher and more stable reward than the goal-conditioned A3C-style GoalNav baseline and far exceeds a random-walk heuristic, below the BFS oracle (Fig. 3). Steps-to-goal grow linearly with straight-line distance. On held-out goal areas, test reward falls from 567 (fine grid, 11% fail) to 293 (medium, 20% fail) and 164 (coarse, 38% fail), against about 623–655 on training goals, while half-trip time stays similar. In Manhattan transfer experiments, pre-training on 4 regions and training only a new goal LSTM on Wall Street approaches joint multi-region training and is only slightly worse than single-city training.
limitations: Not zero-shot: the courier task requires memorising each city, so a new region needs RL retraining (at least a new goal LSTM), and generalisation to large unseen goal areas degrades sharply.
The environment is static (no dynamic agents), the action space is discrete jumps between panoramas, and goals rely on 644 manually defined landmarks and absolute coordinates.
Training is extremely sample-hungry (billions of steps with hundreds of actors), and most results are reported only as learning curves rather than standard success metrics.
